findings.title: Shutdown stops workers before queued work is drained
findings.body: `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` sets each worker's `shutdown` flag before calling `Queue.shutdown(immediate=False)`. `OrderedQueueWorker.run()` checks `while not self.shutdown` at the top of every loop, so a worker that finishes its current item will exit immediately instead of dequeuing the remaining items already in its queue. Since there is exactly one worker per queue, queued work is left unprocessed. This makes the advertised graceful shutdown incorrect and can cause those messages to be delayed or reprocessed after restart/rebalance.

findings.title: Result processor exceptions still mark offsets complete and get committed
findings.body: In `OrderedQueueWorker.run()`, exceptions from `self.result_processor` are caught and logged, but the `finally` block unconditionally calls `self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)`. The commit loop only checks whether offsets are outstanding, so an offset whose processing raised will later be committed as successfully processed. This contradicts the class guarantee that only successful work is committed and can silently drop a message if a result processor ever raises transiently.

findings.title: Shared FixedQueuePool becomes unusable after strategy close and can drop messages on rebalance
findings.body: `ResultsStrategyFactory` creates one `FixedQueuePool` in `__init__`, and each `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` receives that same pool. `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, which shuts down the queues and workers, but `factory.queue_pool` remains non-None. If Arroyo creates a new strategy from the same factory after a rebalance, the new strategy reuses the shut-down pool. `Queue.put()` on a shut-down queue raises `queue.ShutDown`; `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit()` catches all exceptions and marks the offset complete, so messages for the new assignment can be silently dropped.

findings.title: Unbounded queues provide no backpressure and can exhaust memory
findings.body: `FixedQueuePool.__init__` creates each work queue with `queue.Queue()` using the default `maxsize=0`, meaning queues are unbounded. The class doc says there is "natural backpressure when queues fill up," but these queues never fill. If workers process more slowly than the consumer submits, both the queues and the offset-tracking sets grow without bound, eventually risking memory exhaustion or very large commit-lag.

findings.title: OffsetTracker forgets missing offsets after earlier prefix is committed
findings.body: After `mark_committed()` removes offsets <= the committed offset, `get_committable_offsets()` uses `start = max(last_committed + 1, min_offset)`. If offsets 100, 102, and 103 are recorded and 100 is committed, `all_offsets` becomes `{102, 103}`. The next scan starts at 102, so it can commit 103 after 102 and 103 complete even though 101 was never added or processed. This violates the stated rule that all prior offsets must be processed and can skip a genuinely missing message if a real offset gap exists.

findings.title: Concurrent partition insertion can race with commit-loop key iteration
findings.body: `get_committable_offsets()` iterates over `list(self.all_offsets.keys())` without a global lock. `add_offset()` can concurrently insert a new partition key into the same defaultdict. Mutating a dict while iterating over its keys can raise `RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration` (or otherwise produce an inconsistent snapshot), which would interrupt that commit-loop pass. Per-partition locks do not protect the outer key set.
